page_hint: Ch 22 §7 'What We Still Don't Know' vs Ch 22 §6 'Architecture Consequence' and §2 'Mental Model'
quoted_clause: §7: 'Sustained HBM bandwidth for weight-read kernels — discussed in Chapter 2 §7; the 3.35 TB/s H100 figure is a theoretical peak' ... 'Prefill FLOP cost under continuous batching — Chapter 2 §7' ... 'Effect of quantization on decode vs prefill — Chapter 2 §7' ... 'Cross-technology bandwidth numbers — Chapter 2 §7'; §6: 'each GPU streams only ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35 TB/s (Ch 6)'
observed: Within one chapter, the same 3.35 TB/s figure is attributed to two different chapters, and four unrelated open questions are all pointed at a single subsection reference that cannot plausibly own all of them.
evidence: §6 attributes the 3.35 TB/s HBM figure to Ch 6; §7 attributes the same figure to Chapter 2 §7. §2 attributes the prefill/decode split to Ch 2 §2. The four §7 items span bandwidth (Ch 6 territory), prefill FLOPs (Ch 8 territory) and quantization (Ch 7/8 territory) — all pointed at 'Chapter 2 §7'.
root_cause: Chapter numbers appear to have been renumbered after this chapter was written and the §7 pointers were not updated; the §6 pointer was updated.
correction: Re-point each §7 item to the chapter that actually owns the treatment (bandwidth, prefill FLOPs, quantization), and make §6 and §7 agree on where the 3.35 TB/s figure is established.
acceptance_test: Every cross-reference in Ch 22 resolves to a section that contains the cited content; the 3.35 TB/s figure has exactly one home chapter referenced consistently.

page_hint: Ch 22, Figure 22.1 note, 'Prefill is compute-bound' sentence
quoted_clause: ~1.19 PFLOPS required at the ~1.08 s budget
observed: The 1.08 s prefill time budget is used in the rate calculation (1.29/1.08 = 1.19 PFLOPS) but is neither derived in this chapter nor explicitly cross-referenced to its source. The reader encounters it as a given.
evidence: The TTFT SLO is 2 s (p95, Ch 4). The 1.08 s appears to be the prefill component of that budget after subtracting queueing, network, and first-token time, but the decomposition is not shown here. The figure note uses it without a parenthetical like '(Ch 8 §X: prefill allocation from the 2 s TTFT budget)'.
root_cause: The number is likely established in Ch 8 or Ch 14, but the cross-reference is implicit rather than explicit at the point of use.
correction: Add a brief parenthetical at first use: '(~1.08 s prefill allocation from the 2 s TTFT budget, Ch 8 §X)' or similar, so the reader can trace the number without flipping to another chapter.
acceptance_test: A reader encountering the 1.08 s figure for the first time can identify, from the text at that location, which chapter/section establishes it and what the full TTFT decomposition is.

quoted_clause: We established what a token is in Chapter 1 — not a word, character, or byte, but whatever the model's tokenizer carves text into via learned byte-pair merging; that token counts are never proportional to character counts; and that “one token ≈ 4 characters” is a rough rule for general-English prose
observed: Garbled clause: 'that token counts are never proportional to character counts' is not a well-formed statement (token counts are not proportional to character counts — but 'never' also overstates: token counts are approximately proportional to character counts for a fixed tokenizer and language, which is exactly why the 4-chars-per-token rule exists).
evidence: The same chapter's §5 says 'code, numerics, and non-Latin scripts routinely run 2-5x the naive word-count estimate' and §4 says 'real counts differ by language, formatting, code, and tokenizer version' — i.e. the relationship is approximate and language-dependent, not 'never proportional'.
root_cause: A compressed restatement of Ch 1's point lost its qualifier.
correction: Rewrite as 'that token counts are only approximately proportional to character counts, and the ratio depends on language, formatting and tokenizer version'.
acceptance_test: The clause is consistent with the 4-chars-per-token rule stated two sentences later and with §5's language-dependence point.

quoted_clause: The reasoning is traced by the architect and the system investigating together.
observed: The phrase 'the system investigating together' is ambiguous. It could mean (a) the book's reasoning framework, (b) the deployed system under design, or (c) the architect and the system co-investigating. In context the intended meaning is (a), but the sentence reads as if the system is an agent.
evidence: The preceding sentence says 'We do not reach for vendor marketing numbers or rule-of-thumb heuristics. Instead we trace a vague stakeholder ask... through a canonical loop.' The 'system' here most naturally refers to the loop/framework, but the sentence structure makes it read as a co-investigator.
root_cause: Vague noun reference in a transitional sentence.
correction: Rewrite for clarity, e.g., 'The reasoning is traced by the architect using the canonical loop as a structured investigation framework.' Or simply delete the sentence if the preceding paragraph already conveys the point.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify unambiguously what 'the system' refers to without re-reading the paragraph.

quoted_clause: §3: 'the prompt consists of ~1,200 tokens of query text plus ~8,000 tokens of retrieved RAG context'; §8: 'prompts of ~1,200 tokens of internal documents plus ~8K retrieved context'
observed: The canonical 1,200-token component is described differently in the two places (query text vs internal documents), which matters because the mini-case's stakeholder ask is about internal documents.
evidence: The totals agree (9,200) but the composition does not; Ch 23's dialogue has the user pasting 'product specs and contracts' into the prompt, which is the §8 reading.
root_cause: The canonical workload's composition was restated loosely in the mini-case.
correction: Use one description of the 1,200-token component in Ch 22 §3, §8 and Ch 23, and note in Ch 4 Table 4-2 which it is.
acceptance_test: The 1,200-token component is described identically wherever the canonical 9,200-token prompt is decomposed.

quoted_clause: the canonical ~2,000-user, ~10 rps / ~40 rps peak, RAG Q&A, 70B dense FP16 scenario that every other chapter in this handbook cites
observed: 'Every other chapter' is a universal claim. It is plausible that most chapters reference the canonical scenario, but 'every' is strong and may not be literally true (e.g., a chapter on ADR format or red-team methodology might not cite the specific numbers).
evidence: Without the full manuscript, I cannot verify that literally every chapter cites the canonical scenario. The intent is clear (the scenario is the book's through-line), but the universal quantifier is a small overstatement risk.
root_cause: Rhetorical emphasis ('every') slightly exceeding the verifiable claim.
correction: Soften to 'the canonical... scenario that the handbook's chapters cite throughout' or 'that most chapters in this handbook reference.'
acceptance_test: The claim is either verifiably true for every chapter, or the wording is softened to match the actual coverage.

page_hint: Ch 22 Table 22-1 and Ch 24 §3.3 vs. Ch 25 mini-case
quoted_clause: '8-bit KV' (Ch 22, Ch 24) vs. 'FP8 KV' (Ch 25 mini-case)
observed: The same concept (8-bit floating-point KV cache) is labeled '8-bit KV' in Ch 22 and Ch 24 but 'FP8 KV' in Ch 25. While the context always makes clear it is floating-point (byte-halving of FP16), the terminology shift is a minor inconsistency that could confuse a reader scanning across chapters.
evidence: Ch 22: 'at 8-bit KV the same 9.2K context falls to ~12.06 GB'. Ch 24: 'Candidate A: 4×H100 hosts, 8-bit KV'. Ch 25: 'Render the KV cache in FP8 for the long-context decode path.' All refer to the same 1.31 MB/token format.
root_cause: Terminology drift across chapters written at different times.
correction: Standardize on 'FP8 KV' throughout (more precise, distinguishes from INT8), or use '8-bit (FP8) KV' at first mention in each chapter and 'FP8 KV' thereafter. The house convention lists 'FP8/INT8/8-bit' as a check item.
acceptance_test: A global search for '8-bit KV' and 'FP8 KV' returns a consistent usage pattern (one primary term, the other only as a first-mention gloss).

page_hint: Ch 23 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Next Month Customer Portal'
quoted_clause: quality means "resolve the ticket, not just answer" (a capability that rules out the cheaper model) ... The mirrored restatement turns "let's ship AI next month" into "a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s ..."
observed: The mini-case's stated reasoning excludes the cheaper model and then selects a 7B-class model, which is the book's own cheap tier (Ch 20 §7: '70B for complex queries, 7B for quick ones').
evidence: The mini-case's own premise is that the quality bar 'rules out the cheaper model'; the resulting scope is 'a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU'. Either the premise or the conclusion must change, and as written the mini-case does not require the reader to use the chapter's reasoning — it contradicts it.
root_cause: The scenario was written with a generic 'smaller model is insufficient' premise and then given a concrete 7B conclusion without reconciling the two.
correction: Make the premise specific and consistent: either state that the capability bar rules out a sub-7B model (and why 7B suffices), or change the conclusion to a larger model and re-derive the one-GPU feasibility (7B at 500 tokens: 5 rps x 7 TFLOP = 35 TFLOP/s; a 70B at 500 tokens: 5 x 70 TFLOP = 350 TFLOP/s, still inside one H100's 989 TFLOPS peak, so the burst arithmetic must be redone).
acceptance_test: The mini-case's quality premise and its selected model size are consistent, and the burst arithmetic in the conclusion is recomputed for the model actually named.

quoted_clause: **→ Bound 5: the regulated-data requirement makes the local/server tier the primary path ...** [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2) ... **→ Bound 6: cost ceiling — within a self-host budget (Ch16).** [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)
observed: Bounds 5 and 6 are labelled as canonical-scenario facts from Ch 4 Table 4-2, but they are outputs of this dialogue, and the chapter's own provenance note labels the dialogue as a constructed worked example.
evidence: The chapter's §3 preamble: '[ILLUSTRATIVE] (Scenario provenance — a constructed worked-example dialogue, not a secondary source...)'. The canonical scenario (Ch 4 Table 4-2) is the workload definition (users, rps, tokens, SLO, quality set); 'on-prem preferred if at all possible' and 'within a self-host budget' are new facts introduced by this customer.
root_cause: The [canonical scenario] label was applied to all six bounds for uniformity rather than to the ones actually inherited from Ch 4.
correction: Label Bounds 5 and 6 with the dialogue's own provenance ([ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]) and keep [canonical scenario] on Bounds 1-4; if Ch 4 Table 4-2 does carry tier and cost-ceiling rows, cite those rows explicitly.
acceptance_test: Each bound's label matches where the bound actually came from; the dialogue's provenance note and the per-bound labels agree.

page_hint: Ch 23 §6, Fig 23.1 caption and the italic caption beneath it
quoted_clause: *The framing funnel: broad ask → five question gates (problem, success, data, constraints, scope) → confirmed bounds. This dialogue surfaces the six architectural numbers in Table 23-1 (traffic & concurrency, token profile, SLO, quality bar, ops/tier, TCO).*
observed: The figure shows five gates while the chapter's framework is six numbers; the caption asserts the mapping without giving it, so the reader must infer which gate produces which number.
evidence: §1 lists six numbers; Table 23-1 lists six questions; the figure's five gates are named differently (problem, success, data, constraints, scope) from the six numbers (traffic, tokens, SLO, quality, cost, ops).
root_cause: The figure was designed around a five-gate funnel while the chapter's concept was written around six numbers, and the caption was written to bridge the gap without bridging it.
correction: Either relabel the figure's gates to the six numbers, or add the explicit gate-to-number mapping in the caption (e.g. 'traffic & concurrency and token profile come from the problem gate; SLO from success; quality bar from success; ops/tier from data; TCO from constraints').
acceptance_test: The number of gates in the figure and the number of bounds in Table 23-1 are reconciled explicitly in the caption, and a reader can trace each bound to a gate.

quoted_clause: All four items below are **unresolved (evidence pending)**
observed: The text says "All four items" but the table immediately below contains six rows: Cross-entry-point correlation, Adversary adaptivity, Long-term corpus drift, User-driven accidental injection, Economic cost of hardening, Human-in-the-loop evaluation fatigue.
evidence: Count the table rows in §7: 6 rows. The sentence says "four."
root_cause: Stale count after rows were added to the table.
correction: Change "All four items" to "All six items" (or whatever the correct count is after any further edits).
acceptance_test: The number in the sentence matches the number of table rows in §7.

page_hint: Ch 24 §7 'What We Still Don't Know' (table lead-in)
quoted_clause: All four items below are **unresolved (evidence pending)** — each is an open question with a planned investigation, not a settled fact.
observed: The lead-in says four items; the table that follows has six rows.
evidence: Rows: Cross-entry-point correlation; Adversary adaptivity; Long-term corpus drift; User-driven accidental injection; Economic cost of hardening; Human-in-the-loop evaluation fatigue = 6.
root_cause: Two rows were added to the table without updating the sentence that introduces it.
correction: Change 'All four items' to 'All six items' (or 'Every item below').
acceptance_test: The count in the lead-in equals the number of table rows.

quoted_clause: its per-token cost is ~45% lower (fewer host-hours)
observed: The stated reason for the cost difference is 'fewer host-hours' between 4 hosts (Candidate A) and 8 hosts (Candidate B). A 4:8 host ratio yields a 50% reduction in host-hours, not ~45%.
evidence: 4/8 = 0.50, so per-token cost (proportional to host-hours for the same token volume) is 50% lower. The text's own parenthetical '(fewer host-hours)' identifies the sole differentiator as host count, which gives exactly 50%, not 45%. No fixed-cost component or 8-bit-KV throughput adjustment is stated in the reasoning.
root_cause: Arithmetic error or unstated assumption. If the 45% is intentional (e.g., accounting for 8-bit KV allowing ~10% higher effective throughput per host), that reasoning is absent from the text.
correction: Change '~45% lower' to '~50% lower' to match the stated 'fewer host-hours' reasoning (4 vs 8 hosts). Alternatively, if 45% is the intended figure, add the missing reasoning: e.g., '(fewer host-hours; the 8-bit KV also raises per-host effective throughput by ~10%, narrowing the gap slightly)'.
acceptance_test: The per-token cost reduction stated in the text must equal (1 − hosts_A/hosts_B) when the sole stated differentiator is host count, or the text must explicitly state the additional factor that moves the figure from 50% to 45%.

quoted_clause: §1: 'the Red Team probes the system across three domains: 1. Prompt injection ... 2. RAG corruption ... 3. System-level exploits'; §2 table layers: 'Prompt / Retrieval / Tool use / Model behavior / Fleet orchestration'; Fig 24.1 caption: 'Probes sweep three domains (model behavior, tool use, retrieval/RAG)'
observed: The chapter uses three mutually inconsistent taxonomies of the same thing — the Red Team's probe domains — in §1, §2 and the figure caption.
evidence: §1's three domains are prompt injection / RAG corruption / system-level exploits. §2's table has five layers. The figure caption's three domains are model behavior / tool use / retrieval-RAG, which map to none of §1's three groupings one-to-one (model behavior is not one of §1's domains; system-level exploits is not in the caption's list).
root_cause: The chapter's probe taxonomy was restated locally in each section instead of being defined once and referenced.
correction: Define one taxonomy (the §2 five-layer table is the most complete) and have §1 and the Fig 24.1 caption reference it, or state the mapping between the three groupings explicitly in one place.
acceptance_test: A reader can map every domain named in §1, §2 and the Fig 24.1 caption onto a single list without inference; the figure caption's domain names appear in §1 or §2.

page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3, 'Red Team runs the adversarial pass', item 1
quoted_clause: 40 ×1.29 PFLOP ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s
observed: 40 × 1.29 = 51.6, not 51.5. The text displays 1.29 (rounded from 1.288) but computes with 1.288 (40 × 1.288 = 51.52 ≈ 51.5). The displayed multiplication is internally inconsistent at the shown precision.
evidence: 1.29 × 40 = 51.6. 1.288 × 40 = 51.52. The text writes '40 ×1.29 PFLOP ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s', which a reader checking the arithmetic would find off by 0.1.
root_cause: Display rounding (1.29) vs. working precision (1.288) mismatch in the shown equation.
correction: Either write '40 × 1.288 PFLOP ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s' (using the unrounded value in the displayed equation) or write '40 × 1.29 PFLOP ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s' (using the rounded value consistently). The former is preferable since 51.5 is the value used downstream.
acceptance_test: A reader who multiplies the two displayed numbers (40 and 1.29) gets a result consistent with the displayed product (within the shown rounding).

page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3 'The benchmark trap' and its [DERIVED] note
quoted_clause: its per-token cost is ~45% lower (fewer host-hours) ... [DERIVED] — the ~45% per-token cost delta follows from the candidate host-hour difference
observed: A [DERIVED] numeric claim has no derivation, and the naive derivation from the stated inputs gives a different number.
evidence: Candidate A = 4 hosts, Candidate B = 8 hosts. Host-hour ratio 4/8 = 50%, i.e. ~50% lower cost per token at equal served volume — not 45%. A 45% figure would require an unstated intermediate host count (e.g. 4.5 hosts, which is between the 4.07-host prefill floor at 40% MFU and the 5.43-host floor at 30% MFU), which the text does not state.
root_cause: The cost delta was asserted rather than computed, and the label [DERIVED] was applied to a number whose derivation is absent.
correction: Show the derivation (host-hours x $/hr / tokens served for each candidate) and print the resulting percentage, or restate as '~50% fewer host-hours at equal served volume' and label it [ILLUSTRATIVE].
acceptance_test: The percentage is reproducible from the two candidates' host counts and the $/hr figure; the label matches the derivation actually shown.

quoted_clause: plus ~30 GB activations at the peak for this worked example (K+V alone: 2 × 80 layers × 9.2K × 8,192 × 2 B ≈ 24 GB, plus hidden/MLP working tensors ≈ 30 GB total) [DERIVED], giving ≈ 170 GB total derived footprint. ... the ~30 GB is a transient single-request prefill peak, reused across the batch rather than held per request in flight (17 concurrent × 30 GB is not implied) — so the envelope closes as 140 + 436 + 64 = 640, not 670.
observed: The 30 GB figure is 24 GB of per-request KV plus ~6 GB of transient activation, but the parenthetical characterises the whole 30 GB as transient and batch-reused. That is false for the 24 GB KV component, which is precisely what the 436 GB KV budget already holds per request.
evidence: 17 concurrent requests x 24.9 GB = 423 GB ≈ the 436 GB KV budget — so the KV is per-request resident and multiplied by concurrency, exactly as the parenthetical denies. The envelope 140 + 436 + 64 = 640 closes only if the transient part is ~6 GB drawn from the 64 GB reserve; adding a 30 GB 'activations' line that contains 24 GB of KV double-counts the KV against the 436 GB line.
root_cause: A per-request persistent quantity (KV) and a transient quantity (activation/workspace) were summed into one 'activations' figure and then characterised as wholly transient, so the reader cannot tell which envelope line each component belongs to.
correction: Split the derivation into two lines: 'per-request KV at 9.2K = 24.1 GB (already inside the 436 GB KV line)' and 'transient activation/workspace ≈ 6 GB (inside the 64 GB runtime/workspace reserve)'. State that the ADR's single-request arithmetic is not an envelope term.
acceptance_test: The ADR's memory table lists KV and transient workspace on separate lines, each mapped to exactly one envelope line; 140 + 436 + 64 = 640 closes with no quantity appearing twice; and the phrase 'transient ... reused across the batch' is applied only to the ~6 GB component.

quoted_clause: A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores.
observed: The pronoun 'its' is ambiguous: it could refer to A100 (singular) or the 8×H100 host (collective). The technical point (both GPUs support BF16 natively) is correct, but the sentence structure creates a momentary parse ambiguity.
evidence: A100 is a single GPU; 'the 8×H100 host' is a multi-GPU system. 'Its Tensor Cores' most naturally attaches to the nearest singular noun (A100), but the parenthetical includes the H100 host as well.
root_cause: Sentence structure with a parenthetical that changes the referent.
correction: Rewrite: 'Both A100 and H100 natively support BF16 and TF32 on their Tensor Cores; no next-generation GPU is required.'
acceptance_test: The sentence unambiguously attributes BF16/TF32 support to both GPU types without a dangling pronoun.

page_hint: Ch 26 §2 (definition of [1P]) vs Appendix A 'Quantization implementation observations', 'Intel backend supplement', 'Video systems snapshot'
quoted_clause: **[1P]** marks a first-party **source** — the original method paper authored by the method's creators, or a hardware-vendor specification (technical report, model card, or official documentation). ... [1P][FACT] ([NVFP4 CUTLASS](...)) ... At the pinned revision in the source ledger, `block_q4_K` occupies 144 bytes for 256 values ... The retrieved release APIs identify PyTorch v2.14.1 (September 30), vLLM v0.32.0 (October 18), SGLang v0.5.22 (October 19) ... Official release metadata: [A-S72]
observed: The appendix labels source-code observations (vLLM and llama.cpp files at pinned commits), release-metadata observations (PyTorch / vLLM / SGLang / OpenVINO / Diffusers release dates), API documentation and blog posts as [1P]. Under Ch 26 §2's definition, [1P] covers only (a) an original method paper by the method's creators and (b) a hardware-vendor specification — none of which covers a vLLM source file or a PyTorch release timestamp. The definition and the usage disagree.
evidence: Ch 26 §2: 'Keep the four categories distinct: (a) an original method paper by the method's creators, (b) a hardware-vendor specification, (c) a third-party evaluation ..., and (d) an own measured run ... Of these, [1P] covers (a) and (b) only'. Appendix A applies [1P] to code and release metadata as listed above.
root_cause: Ch 26 §2's definition was written for hardware and method claims and was not generalised to software-artifact provenance, which the appendix's October notes require.
correction: Broaden the Ch 26 §2 definition to 'a first-party artifact from the party that produces the thing — the method's own paper, the vendor's technical report / model card / datasheet, the project's own source code at a pinned revision, or its own release notes and documentation', and state that a code or release-metadata observation is a fact about the artifact, not about deployed performance. Alternatively introduce a distinct provenance token for source-code observations.
acceptance_test: Every [1P] use in Appendix A falls under the Ch 26 §2 definition as amended; a reader can classify each appendix citation from the definition without ambiguity.

quoted_clause: Before selecting patterns, the architect reads the capstone's workload against Fig 26.1 — short prompt, latency-sensitive, moderate quality — and consults the §26.2.1 matrix, which points to the cache + breaker combination.
observed: The capstone is explicitly a distinct short-prompt workload, not the canonical 9.2K RAG case. Fig 26.1's described families are long-context RAG Q&A (context-heavy, latency 0.40), chat (traffic/latency-sensitive, long outputs), and batch (cost-sensitive, latency-tolerant). None matches 'short prompt, latency-sensitive, moderate quality' RAG, and the matrix has no row that points to semantic response cache + circuit breaker for that fingerprint.
evidence: §2.1 provenance note: 'RAG Q&A is quality- and context-heavy with short outputs; chat is traffic- and latency-sensitive with long outputs; batch inference is cost-sensitive and latency-tolerant.' Matrix rows list strategies; no cache+breaker row for short-prompt RAG. Step 1: 'The capstone declares a distinct short-prompt workload — it is not the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case of Ch 4.'
root_cause: The capstone's workload was changed to a short-prompt case but the fingerprint/matrix reference was not updated.
correction: Either add a 'short-prompt RAG / support' row to the matrix and include its fingerprint in Fig 26.1, or reword Step 0: 'The capstone is a new short-prompt RAG workload; use the matrix's method to locate its dominant constraint (latency/queueing under the TTFT SLO), which motivates evaluating response caching and load shedding, rather than claiming the existing matrix points to that combination.'
acceptance_test: The reader can trace the capstone's stated fingerprint to a matrix row or to an explicit method step; no claim that an existing row points to cache+breaker unless such a row exists.
